summary: A clever youth enters into a wager with a woman who is having an affair with a neighbor while her husband is deaf. Through a series of ingenious tricks and psychological manipulations, he forces the woman to confess her infidelity, winning the wager and exposing the truth.
full_text:
TOM TOTHERHOUSE

Once on a time there was a Goody who had a deaf husband. A good, easy man he was, but that was just why she thought more of the lad next door, whom they called 'Tom Totherhouse'. Now the lad that served the deaf man saw very well that the two had something between them, and one day he said to the Goody: 'Dare you wager ten dollars, mother, that I don’t make you lay bare your own shame?' 

'Yes I dare', said she; snip and so they wagered ten dollars. So one day, while the lad and the deaf man stood thrashing in the barn, the lad saw that Tom Totherhouse came to see the Goody. He said nothing, but a good while before dinnertime he turned toward the barn-door, and bawled out 'Halloa!' 

'What! are we to go home already?' said the man, who hadn’t given any heed to what the lad did. 'Yes, we must, since mother calls', said the lad. So when they got into the passage, the lad began to hem and cough, that the Goody might get Tom Totherhouse out of the way. But when they came into the room, there stood a whole bowl of custards on the table. 'Nay, nay, mother', cried out the man; snip 'shall we have custards to-day?' 

'Yes, that you shall, dear', said the Goody; snip but she was as sour as verjuice, and as cross as two sticks. So when they had eaten and drank all the good cheer up, off they went again to their work, and the Goody said to Tom: 'Deil take that lad’s sharp nose, this was all his fault; snip but now you must be off as fast as you can, and I’ll come down to you in the mead with a snack between meals.' 

This the lad stood outside in the passage and listened to. 'Do you know, father', he said, 'I think we’d best go down into the hollow and put our fence to rights, which is blown down, before the neighbours’ swine get in and root up our meadow.' 'Aye, aye, let’s go and do it', said the man; snip for he did all he was told, good, easy man. 

So when the afternoon was half spent, down came the Goody sneaking along into the mead, with something under her apron. 'Nay, nay, mother', said the man, 'it can’t be you any longer; snip are we to have a snack between meals too?' 'Yes, yes, that you shall', she said; snip but she was sourer and wilder than ever. 

So they made merry, and crammed themselves with bannocks and butter, and had a drop of brandy into the bargain. 'I’ll go off to Tom Totherhouse with a snack—shan’t I, mother?' said the lad. 'He’s had nothing between meals, I’ll be bound.' 'Ah! do; snip there’s a good fellow', said the Goody, who all at once got as mild as milk. 

As he went along the lad broke a bannock to bits, and dropped the crumbs here and there as he walked. But when he got to Tom Totherhouse he said: 'Now, just you take care, for our old cock has found out that you come too often to see our Goody. He won’t stand it any longer, and has sworn to drive his axe into you as soon as ever he can set eyes on you.' 

As for Tom, he was so frightened he scarce knew which way to turn, and the lad went back again to his master. 'There’s something wrong', he said, 'with Tom’s plough, and he begs you to be so good as to take your axe, and go and see if you can’t set it right.' Yes, the man set off with his axe, but Tom Totherhouse had scarce caught sight of him before he took to his heels as fast as he could. The man turned and twisted the plough round and round, and looked at it on every side, and when he couldn’t see anything wrong with it he went off home again; snip but on the way he picked up the bits of broken bannock which the lad had let fall. His old dame stood in the meadow and looked at him as he did this for a while, and wondered and wondered what it could be her husband was gathering up. 

'Oh, I know', said the lad, 'master’s picking up stones, I’ll be bound; snip for he has marked how often this Tom Totherhouse runs over here; snip and the old fellow won’t stand it any longer; snip and now he has sworn to stone mother to death.' 

Off went the Goody as fast as her legs could carry her. 'Ah! ah! don’t stone me to death; snip don’t stone me to death! and I’ll give you my word never to let Tom Totherhouse come near me again.' 

'Now the ten dollars are mine', bawled out the lad; snip and so they were.
moral: Dishonesty and betrayal will eventually be uncovered by a keen mind.

title: The Twelve Wild Ducks
summary: A queen exchanges her twelve sons for a daughter, who grows up to seek her brothers. She discovers they are transformed into wild ducks and spends years weaving magical clothes to break their curse.
full_text: Once on a time there was a Queen who, desiring a daughter, traded her twelve sons to a Troll in exchange for a daughter, Snow-white and Rosy-red. As the princess grew, she learned of her lost brothers and set off to find them. She discovered they lived in a wooden hut and were transformed into wild ducks every morning. To break the spell, she had to pick thistle-down and weave twelve coats, shirts, and neckerchiefs without talking, laughing, or weeping. Despite the interference of a king who fell in love with her and a jealous stepmother who tried to frame her for eating her own children, the princess completed the task. Her brothers were restored to human form, and she lived happily with the king.
moral: Unwavering love and determination can overcome the most difficult of trials.

title: True and Untrue
summary: Two brothers, True and Untrue, leave home. Untrue blinds his brother and leaves him, but True recovers his sight and uses secrets learned from animals to win the king's favor and a princess.
full_text: Two brothers, True and Untrue, set out to find their fortune. Untrue betrays True by stealing his food and eventually plucking out his eyes. While blind, True climbs a tree and overhears animals discussing cures for the King of England's ailments: dew for his blindness, a toad for his daughter's muteness, and a spring under a stone for his water. True uses these secrets to cure the King and the Princess, gaining wealth and a royal marriage. Untrue eventually returns, pretending to be a beggar, but is outwitted by True and left with nothing, as his nature remains fundamentally untrue.
moral: Honesty and goodness are eventually rewarded, while deceit leads to ruin.

title: Tatterhood
summary: A girl dressed in rags and underestimated by society possesses profound wisdom and courage. Through a series of trials, she solves complex riddles and saves a kingdom, proving that intellect and heart are more valuable than fine clothing.
full_text: There was once a girl who was so poorly dressed that everyone called her Tatterhood. She was mocked for her rags, but she possessed a mind sharper than any sword. One day, a prince was placed under a curse that only the most intelligent person in the land could break. Many lords and scholars tried and failed. Tatterhood, though dismissed by the court, stepped forward and solved the riddles that had baffled the wise. Through her insight and bravery, she broke the curse and restored the kingdom's peace. The prince, captivated by her wisdom and spirit, married her, and she became a beloved queen, teaching all that appearance is no measure of a person's worth.
moral: True value resides in character and intellect, not in outward appearance or social status.

title: Three Years without Wages
summary: A youth serves a miserly master for three years without pay, receiving only a puppy, a kitten, and a lizard as his wages. He discovers the animals are transformed royalty and, with their help, attains a magical ring and a kingdom.
full_text: A lazy youth was hired as a ploughboy by a rich man on the condition that he serve three years without wages. In return, the master promised to buy him three things—the first items he encountered in town on three separate mornings. The youth received a puppy, a kitten, and a lizard. He soon discovered the lizard was actually a prince under a witch's spell. After saving the prince, the youth was gifted a magical ring that granted any wish. Using the ring, he outsmarted the miserly master and the king, eventually marrying a princess and ruling a prosperous land, proving that patience and kindness are rewarded.
moral: Persistence and an open heart toward the unlikely can lead to rewards far greater than material wages.

title: The Tallow Candle
summary: A poetic story told from the perspective of a tallow candle, reflecting on the fleeting nature of life, light, and the inevitable end.
full_text: In the rich tradition of Danish folklore, the tale of The Tallow Candle is told. A poetic story told from the perspective of a tallow candle, reflecting on the fleeting nature of life, light, and the inevitable end. This story has been passed down through generations, reflecting the values and fears of the people of Denmark, weaving together the mundane and the magical in a way that captures the essence of the Nordic spirit.
moral: Life is full of mysteries that demand our respect.

title: The Tinderbox
summary: A soldier finds a magic tinderbox that allows him to summon three powerful dogs made of precious metals, leading him to wealth and a princess.

title: The Trolls of Reynisdrangar
summary: Two trolls attempted to pull a great three-masted ship to the shore of the black sand beach of Reynisfjara. However, they were too slow, and as the sun rose over the horizon, the sunlight hit them, instantly turning them into the towering basalt sea stacks that still stand today as a warning against the power of the sun.
full_text: In the ancient lands of Iceland, the story of The Trolls of Reynisdrangar has been told for generations. Two trolls attempted to pull a great three-masted ship to the shore of the black sand beach of Reynisfjara. However, they were too slow, and as the sun rose over the horizon, the sunlight hit them, instantly turning them into the towering basalt sea stacks that still stand today as a warning against the power of the sun. This legend serves as a reminder of the mysterious forces that once governed the north, where the boundary between the mundane and the supernatural was as thin as a winter's frost. The echoes of these events still linger in the wind and the stone, whispering to those who know how to listen.
moral: Respect the unseen forces of the world.

title: The Treasure of Skógafoss
summary: Legend tells of a wealthy man named Þrasi Þórólfsson who buried a chest filled with gold and valuables behind the curtain of water at the Skógafoss waterfall. For centuries, people have searched for the treasure, and it is said that only those with a pure heart can find the spot where the gold remains hidden.

title: The Terror of the Yule Cat
summary: The Yule Cat is a giant, monstrous feline that prowls the Icelandic countryside during the winter solstice. It is said that the cat eats anyone who has not received a new piece of clothing for Christmas, a legend that historically encouraged the completion of wool production before the end of the year.

title: The Tale of the Völva
summary: A powerful Völva, or seeress, is summoned to a chieftain's court to predict the future of the land. Through a ritual of chanting and trance, she reveals a vision of coming wars and natural disasters, reminding the people that the threads of fate are woven by the Norns and cannot be undone.

title: The Trolls of the Lava Fields
summary: The vast lava fields of the south are said to be the remains of trolls who were caught by the dawn. These creatures spent their nights carving the land and building fortresses, but the first light of the sun turned their skin to basalt, leaving them as permanent, frozen monuments in the stone.

title: The Tale of the Silver Salmon
summary: A fisherman catches a shimmering silver salmon that can speak. The fish promises to grant him one wish in exchange for its freedom. The man asks for the ability to understand the language of all animals, which allows him to uncover a plot to overthrow the local chieftain.

title: The Tale of Kagsagsuk
summary: Kagsagsuk is a mistreated orphan boy who suffers extreme cruelty from his foster mother and the village men. Seeking strength, he journeys to the mountains to encounter the Amarok, a giant solitary wolf spirit. Through a series of grueling trials where the Amarok repeatedly throws him down, Kagsagsuk sheds his weaknesses and gains superhuman strength. He eventually returns to the village, defeats three bears, and takes revenge on those who tormented him, though he remains a lonely figure of legend.
full_text: Kagsagsuk was an orphan, small and weak, who lived with a foster mother who despised him. She fed him scraps, dressed him in rags, and sent him to sleep in the dog pen where the huskies curled against the wind. The village men mocked him, calling him useless, and the children threw stones at him when he passed. But Kagsagsuk dreamed of strength. One night, as the northern lights painted the sky in curtains of green and violet, he decided to leave the village forever. He walked into the mountains, his thin clothes offering no protection against the wind, and climbed until he reached a high valley where the snow was stained red at dawn. There he met the Amarok, the great wolf spirit, larger than any bear, with fur gray as storm clouds and eyes like burning coals. 'You seek strength, little one?' the Amarok growled, its voice shaking the ground. 'Then let us begin.' The Amarok charged. Kagsagsuk tried to stand his ground, but the wolf threw him down the slope, tumbling over rocks and ice. He rose, bruised and bleeding. The Amarok threw him again, harder this time, and Kagsagsuk felt bones crack. 'Again!' the wolf commanded. Kagsagsuk rose once more, and on the third throw, he felt something shift inside him. Weakness fell away like old bones shedding flesh. His arms grew thick, his legs became pillars, and his heart hardened into a drum of war. 'Now you are ready,' said the Amarok, and vanished into the storm. Kagsagsuk returned to the village a changed man. He found three great bears terrorizing the settlement, and with his bare hands, he killed them all, stacking their pelts at the feet of the elders. His foster mother wept in terror. But Kagsagsuk did not harm her. He simply turned and walked away, leaving the village to its shame. He became a legendary figure of the wild, a protector of the helpless who never again trusted the kindness of men.
moral: True strength is forged through suffering; forgiveness is the ultimate power over those who wronged you.

title: Tiggak the Shaman
summary: Tiggak is a powerful angakkoq (shaman) who becomes lazy and neglects his duties, causing friction with his brothers-in-law. During a harsh winter, the group becomes stranded on dangerous ice floes. Tiggak's supernatural foresight and magical abilities become the group's only hope for survival. By invoking charms and navigating the treacherous landscape with mystical guidance, he saves his companions, proving that his wisdom is indispensable despite his personal failings.
full_text: Tiggak was an angakkoq of formidable power, a shaman whose spirit could travel to the moon and whose word could calm the sea. But he was also lazy, preferring to sleep while others worked, and his brothers-in-law resented him deeply. 'Your magic does not fill our bellies,' they complained. The tension came to a head during a winter so brutal that the seals vanished. The brothers-in-law prepared to travel to a distant hunting ground, and Tiggak insisted on joining them. The journey was treacherous from the start. A storm swept in from the east, and the ice pack began to break apart. The men scrambled onto a drifting floe, their supplies lost, their kayaks smashed. As night fell and the wolves howled from the shore, the brothers-in-law began to despair. But Tiggak sat cross-legged on the ice and began to chant. The sky above them began to clear, and a beam of moonlight illuminated a path through the broken ice. 'Follow the light,' Tiggak said. They walked for hours, jumping from floe to floe. Whenever one of the brothers-in-law slipped, Tiggak caught them with a gesture. When a polar bear emerged from the darkness, Tiggak held up his hand and the bear turned and walked away. They reached the shore at dawn, exhausted but alive. The brothers-in-law never again spoke ill of Tiggak.
moral: Even imperfect people possess irreplaceable gifts; wisdom often comes in unexpected forms.

title: The Theft of Daylight
summary: In a time of eternal darkness, the world was cold and blind. Raven, the cunning trickster, discovered that a powerful being held the light of the world captured in a box. Through a series of disguises and tricks, Raven managed to steal the light and release it into the sky, creating the sun, moon, and stars, and bringing warmth and visibility to the Inuit people.
full_text: In the time before time, the world was wrapped in endless darkness. Raven saw the suffering and decided to help. He flew until he reached the house of a great chief who possessed three boxes containing the sun, the moon, and the stars. Raven transformed into a pine needle and floated into the chief's drinking water. The chief's daughter drank and became pregnant, giving birth to a baby boy who was Raven in disguise. The chief adored his grandson. One day, the baby pointed at the chest and cried until the chief opened it, releasing the stars. The next day, he released the moon. The next day, the sun blazed into the sky. The people wept with joy. Raven transformed back and flew away, cackling. And the light was in the sky, never to be put back in its box.
moral: Cleverness and patience can achieve what strength alone cannot.

title: The Transformation of Raven
summary: An origin story explaining why the Raven is black. Originally, Raven had beautiful shimmering feathers, but through a series of mishaps and his own trickery, he was scorched by fire or covered in soot. This transformation serves as a permanent mark of his trickster nature.
full_text: Raven was not always black. He had feathers of every color — blues, greens, golds, reds, purples. He was the most beautiful bird in creation, and he knew it. His vanity was legendary. One day, Raven flew through a canyon and saw smoke rising from a crack. Curious, he flew closer, and soot blackened his wingtips. But his vanity drove him back to the fire again and again, trying to remove the soot, and each time more feathers turned black. Soon all his magnificent colors were gone. Raven wept, but the colors never returned. 'You were given beauty,' the spirits told him, 'but you used it only to serve yourself. Now black you shall remain, to remind all who look upon you that beauty without kindness is a hollow thing.'
moral: Beauty without kindness is hollow; vanity leaves a permanent mark.

title: Tikta'Liktak's Journey Home
summary: A young hunter becomes stranded on a drifting ice floe. The story chronicles his struggle for survival and encounters with Arctic spirits. His return home is a testament to navigation skills and the spiritual connection between a hunter and his homeland.
full_text: Tikta'Liktak set out alone, chasing a seal that led him farther from shore. When he looked up, the shore had vanished. The ice floe had broken free. For seven days he drifted, eating raw seal meat. On the third day, a walrus spoke: 'Follow the star that never moves.' On the fifth, a polar bear said: 'Do not eat all your meat at once.' On the seventh, a raven said: 'The wind will carry you home.' He navigated by the North Star, conserved his food, and read the wind. When the current brought him close to land, he jumped and swam. He collapsed at his mother's feet. He taught every young hunter to read the stars, conserve strength, and respect the ice.
moral: The land tests those who take it for granted; survival is earned through respect and knowledge.

title: The Tickling Demon Mahaha
summary: Mahaha is a thin, ice-blue demon who tickles victims with long nails until they die from lack of breath. However, the story concludes that Mahaha can be outwitted by the clever, who eventually trap him in a water hole.
full_text: Mahaha is a demon with skin the blue of old ice and claws as long as knives. He does not stab or crush. He tickles. He sneaks up on victims and tickles them until they cannot breathe, dying with a smile frozen on their face. But Mahaha has a weakness. He cannot resist hearing his name spoken backward. One clever hunter shouted 'AHAHAM!' into the darkness. Mahaha froze. The hunter ran to a water hole and jumped in. Mahaha followed, and the hunter swam through an underwater passage, emerging safely while Mahaha remained trapped beneath the ice.
moral: Even the most terrifying foe has a weakness waiting to be discovered.

title: The Tale of Njunje Paggas
summary: A Stállu tale collected by P. A. Lindholm and illustrated by John Bauer. Njunje Paggas is a Sámi hero who faces the Stállu in a battle of wits. The Stállu is a large, human-like creature who eats people. The Sámi hero wins through cleverness rather than strength. The Stállu's own knife must not be used against him, or he gains strength.
full_text: Njunje Paggas was a Sámi of ordinary size but extraordinary cleverness. When the Stállu began stealing reindeer from his family's herd, Njunje Paggas decided to confront the giant. He found the Stállu sitting outside his cave, gnawing on a reindeer leg. 'You have been taking my family's reindeer,' Njunje Paggas said. The Stállu laughed. 'I take what I want. What will you do about it, little man?' Njunje Paggas challenged the Stállu to a contest of wits. 'If I can trick you three times,' he said, 'you must leave our lands forever. If you trick me three times, I will bring you a hundred reindeer.' The Stállu agreed, confident in his cunning. The first trick: Njunje Paggas told the Stállu there was a golden reindeer in the forest and led him to a pond where the moon reflected like gold. The Stállu reached for it and fell in. The second trick: Njunje Paggas convinced the Stállu to let him tie him to a tree 'to keep him safe from the golden reindeer' while he 'searched for more.' The third trick: Njunje Paggas used his own knife, not the Stállu's, to carve a branch so it looked like the Stállu's head, convincing him he had been beheaded. The Stállu, terrified, fled the lands forever, and Njunje Paggas became a hero celebrated in stories and songs.
moral: Three clever tricks are worth more than an army of strong warriors.
source: P. A. Lindholm; Conrad, JoAnn (2020), Folklore 131:2

title: Trøllanes and the Troll House Party
summary: The settlement of Trøllanes on Kalsoy Island takes its name from ancient trolls who would come ashore once a year to wreak havoc—eating all available food, drinking, dancing, and behaving like wild party-goers. Terrified villagers would flee to Mikladalur every year, leaving their homes to be ransacked. One year, a woman was unable to escape and hid under a table as the trolls danced and feasted above her. In terror, she exclaimed 'Christ!' The trolls, hearing the holy name, fled from the village in panic and never returned. The route to the Kallur lighthouse begins in Trøllanes, offering some of the most dramatic views in the Faroe Islands.
full_text:
The settlement of Trøllanes on Kalsoy Island takes its name from ancient trolls who would come ashore once a year to wreak havoc — eating all available food, drinking, dancing, and behaving like wild party-goers. The name itself means 'Troll Ness' or 'Troll Peninsula,' and the settlers who chose to live there centuries ago must have known the reputation of the place. The village sits at the end of a long, narrow valley, sheltered by towering cliffs that funnel the wind into eerie howls — a sound that the old people said was the trolls laughing.

Terrified villagers would flee to Mikladalur every year, leaving their homes to be ransacked. They took what they could carry — food stores, precious tools, children — and retreated to the safety of the neighboring village, locking doors and shuttering windows behind them. But locks and shutters meant nothing to trolls. By morning, the houses were wrecked, the food was gone, and the trolls had moved on, leaving only footprints the size of boats pressed into the mud.

One year, a woman was unable to escape and hid under a table as the trolls danced and feasted above her. The floor shook. The dishes rattled. The trolls sang in voices like grinding stone and laughed with mouths full of food. She could smell them — a sharp, animal scent of wet fur and old earth. In terror, she exclaimed 'Christ!' The trolls, hearing the holy name, fled from the village in panic and never returned. The holy name was their undoing, and Trøllanes was freed. The route to the Kallur lighthouse begins in Trøllanes, offering some of the most dramatic views in the Faroe Islands — a landscape that still feels like troll country.
moral: Folklore preserves the wisdom of a people.

title: Trøllkonufingur (The Troll Woman's Finger)
summary: A giant troll-woman from Iceland came to Vágar Island with the same plan as Risin and Kellingin: to steal the Faroe Islands and drag them to Iceland. Like the giants, she could only work at night. Caught by sunrise, sunlight turned her to stone. She toppled from the cliff into the sea—and was so enormous that her head became the island of Koltur (inhabited by only two people, Bjørn and Lukka Patursson), while one finger remained above water as the rock formation Trøllkonufingur near Sandavagur. Visible from the airport, it is a popular climbing spot. In 1844, a member of the Royal Danish entourage climbed it, descended, realized he'd dropped a glove, climbed back up—and was never seen again.
full_text:
A giant troll-woman from Iceland came to Vágar Island with the same plan as Risin and Kellingin: to steal the Faroe Islands and drag them to Iceland. She crossed the sea at night, swimming through water so cold it would kill a human in minutes, her massive body cutting through the waves like a ship's hull. Like the giants, she could only work at night — sunlight was her enemy, the one force that could undo her plans.

She reached Vágar Island and began to search for a rope strong enough to bind the islands together. But she moved too slowly. The work was harder than she expected, the islands heavier than they looked. She searched the cliffs for the right binding point, her fingers scraping the rock, leaving grooves that can still be seen today.

Caught by sunrise, sunlight turned her to stone. She toppled from the cliff into the sea — and was so enormous that her head became the island of Koltur, while one finger remained above water as the rock formation Trøllkonufingur near Sandavágur. The finger stands like a jagged monument, pointing accusingly at the sky that betrayed her.

Koltur is inhabited by only two people, Bjørn and Lukka Patursson, who live in the shadow of a petrified giantess. The rock formation is visible from the airport, and it is a popular climbing spot — though climbing it is not for the faint-hearted. In 1844, a member of the Royal Danish entourage climbed it, descended, realized he had dropped a glove, climbed back up — and was never seen again. Some say the troll-woman's spirit still guards her finger, punishing those who dare to scale it.
moral: Pride and greed are punished by nature itself.

title: Tórur Rami and the Three Gifts of Mykines
summary: A giant named Tórur Rami tried to conquer the island of Mykines. The native inhabitant Óli Rami opposed him. When the giant approached, Óli Rami used magic to split Mykineshólmur from the main island, creating the islet now reached by a narrow metal bridge. The giant jumped across and they fought. Óli Rami won and spared the giant's life in exchange for three gifts: (1) a great whale would appear annually in Hvalagjógv bay—but the people complained and it stopped; (2) a giant magical tree—but the people complained it was shabby and it withered; (3) gannets (seabirds) that still nest only on Mykineshólmur. The condition was that the people must never complain about the gifts.
full_text:
A giant named Tórur Rami tried to conquer the island of Mykines. He was a brute of a thing — taller than the sea stacks, with hands like boulders and a voice that shook the cliffs when he spoke. The native inhabitant Óli Rami opposed him, though he was no giant. What Óli Rami lacked in size he made up for in cunning and magic, gifts passed down through generations of island dwellers who had learned to survive in a land of storms and stone.

When the giant approached, Óli Rami used magic to split Mykineshólmur from the main island, creating the islet now reached by a narrow metal bridge. The sea rushed in to fill the gap, and the giant was stranded on the opposite shore, howling with rage. But he was not finished. He jumped across the gap — a leap that would kill any human — and they fought.

Óli Rami won and spared the giant's life in exchange for three gifts: a great whale would appear annually in Hvalagjógv bay — but the people complained about the smell and it stopped; a giant magical tree — but the people complained it was shabby and it withered; gannets that still nest only on Mykineshólmur, their white bodies covering the cliffs like snow. The condition was that the people must never complain about the gifts.

The gannets remain. The whale and the tree are gone, lost to human ingratitude. The lesson of Mykines is simple: the world offers wonders, but only if you accept them without complaint.
moral: Folklore preserves the wisdom of a people.

title: Tróndur í Gøtu (Tróndur the Viking Chieftain)
summary: Tróndur í Gøtu was a powerful 10th-century Viking chieftain who lived in Gøta on Eysturoy. He is the central figure in the Færeyinga Saga, which recounts his fierce opposition to the Christianization of the islands. He led pagan resistance against Sigmundur Brestisson, who was sent by King Olaf Tryggvason of Norway to convert the Faroese. After a series of battles, Sigmundur ultimately won and killed Tróndur. However, in folklore, Tróndur is often portrayed as a tragic hero—a symbol of Faroese independence and resistance against foreign domination. His burial mound is said to exist near Gøta.
full_text:
Tróndur í Gøtu was a powerful 10th-century Viking chieftain who lived in Gøta on Eysturoy, in a longhouse overlooking the narrow sound where the sea rushes in at high tide. He is the central figure in the Færeyinga Saga, which recounts his fierce opposition to the Christianization of the islands — a struggle that was as much about political power as it was about faith.

He led pagan resistance against Sigmundur Brestisson, who was sent by King Olaf Tryggvason of Norway to convert the Faroese by force. Tróndur refused. He had served the old gods all his life — Thor, Odin, Freyja — and he would not abandon them for a foreign god brought by foreign warriors. The battles between Tróndur and Sigmundur were fierce, fought across the islands in the long summer months when the sea was calm enough to travel.

After a series of battles, Sigmundur ultimately won and killed Tróndur. But in folklore, Tróndur is often portrayed as a tragic hero — a symbol of Faroese independence and resistance against foreign domination. His burial mound is said to exist near Gøta, a low, grass-covered hill that locals still avoid at night. Some say his ghost walks the shore, still guarding the islands he refused to surrender.
moral: Folklore preserves the wisdom of a people.

title: The Troll Who Captured a Princess
summary: A classic Faroese folk tale collected by Jakob Jakobsen tells of a troll who lived in a cave and captured a princess to pick lice from his hair. Three brothers set out to rescue her. The elder two brothers failed, but the youngest—helped by the princess who threw him a ball of yarn to track the cave entrance—confronted the troll. The troll tried to trick the boy but was outwitted. When the troll gained entry to the king's house by picking the Faroese wooden lock (hvölpalás), the boy killed him. The treacherous brothers claimed credit, but the princess revealed the truth. The youngest brother married the princess and became king. Faroese trolls are creatures of darkness, large and ugly but easily outwitted.
full_text:
A classic Faroese folk tale collected by Jakob Jakobsen tells of a troll who lived in a cave high in the mountains and captured a princess to pick lice from his hair. The princess was taken from her father's kingdom — a land of green valleys and stone churches — and carried through the mountains in the troll's massive arms, her screams lost in the wind. She was set to work in the dark cave, picking lice from the troll's tangled hair while he slept.

Three brothers set out to rescue her. The elder two brothers failed — one was tricked by the troll's riddles, the other lost his way in the mountains and was never found. But the youngest — helped by the princess who threw him a ball of yarn to track the cave entrance — confronted the troll. The troll tried to trick the boy but was outwitted, outplayed by a child who had nothing but courage and a length of string.

When the troll gained entry to the king's house by picking the Faroese wooden lock (hvölpalás), the boy killed him. The treacherous brothers claimed credit, but the princess revealed the truth. The youngest brother married the princess and became king. Faroese trolls are creatures of darkness, large and ugly but easily outwitted — a reminder that intelligence and courage matter more than size and strength.
moral: Courage and cleverness triumph over brute strength.
source: Jakob Jakobsen - Færöske Folkesagn og Æventyr; John F. West translation

title: Tippafossur and the Killing of Jógvan
summary: A grim legend within the Ormur cycle. Jógvan, a farmer from Oyri, caught Ormur of Skála stealing his sheep and attacked him. Miraculously, Jógvan overpowered the huge Ormur and held him down, calling for his son to bring a knife. But the son, terrified of Ormur, fled and hid at the Tippafossur gorge. Ormur, pinned and fearing death, promised the devil a piece of his little finger in exchange for strength. Suddenly gaining supernatural power, Ormur broke free and killed Jógvan. He then found the boy at Tippafossur and killed him too. Later, in his sleep, Ormur muttered: 'The clothes lie under the corn and the bodies under Tippafossur.' His farmhands heard, found the evidence, and informed the authorities.
full_text:
A grim legend within the Ormur cycle. Jógvan, a farmer from Oyri, caught Ormur of Skála stealing his sheep and attacked him. Miraculously, Jógvan overpowered the huge Ormur and held him down, calling for his son to bring a knife. The scene played out on the hillside above Tippafossur, where the gorge drops away to the sea in a sheer cliff of black basalt.

But the son, terrified of Ormur, fled and hid at the Tippafossur gorge. He could hear his father's shouts echoing across the valley, but he could not move. Ormur's reputation had preceded him — tales of violence and cruelty that had been whispered in every farmhouse on Eysturoy.

Ormur, pinned and fearing death, promised the devil a piece of his little finger in exchange for strength. Suddenly gaining supernatural power, Ormur broke free and killed Jógvan. He then found the boy at Tippafossur and killed him too, the bodies falling into the gorge where the sea could claim them.

Later, in his sleep, Ormur muttered: 'The clothes lie under the corn and the bodies under Tippafossur.' His farmhands heard, found the evidence, and informed the authorities. Ormur was eventually caught, his Achilles' tendon severed by a thrown knife, and executed. He is buried at Stevnuválur overlooking the lands where he committed his crimes — a monument to the darkness that can live in a human heart.
moral: Evil deeds eventually come to light.

title: The Tomtegubbe – Åland's Household Guardian
summary: The tomte (or gårdstomte) is a household spirit who lives on farms and in barns, watching over the family and livestock. On Åland, as in the rest of the Swedish-speaking world, the tomte was both protector and disciplinarian: he rewarded hard work and good management with prosperity, but punished laziness, drunkenness, and night work with mischief or outright harm. The tomte expected to be fed — typically a bowl of porridge with butter on Christmas Eve. If neglected, he would cause accidents, make the cows go dry, or leave the farm entirely. The tradition is preserved in the annual children's anthology 'Bland tomtar och troll' (Among Gnomes and Trolls), first published in 1907 and still going today, which features stories collected from across the Swedish language area including Åland. The tomte represents the moral code of the traditional Åland farming community, where hard work and respect for the unseen were paramount.
full_text:
The tomte is a household spirit who lives on farms and in barns, watching over the family and livestock with a fierce, unblinking devotion. On Åland, as in the rest of the Swedish-speaking world, the tomte was both protector and disciplinarian: he rewarded hard work and good management with prosperity, but punished laziness, drunkenness, and night work with mischief or outright harm. The tomte was not a creature to be trifled with — he was ancient, patient, and possessed of a moral clarity that left no room for excuses.

The tomte expected to be fed — typically a bowl of porridge with butter on Christmas Eve, left on the doorstep or in the barn. If neglected, he would cause accidents, make the cows go dry, or leave the farm entirely, taking his luck and protection with him. Some families claimed to hear their tomte's footsteps on the roof during winter storms, or to see his small, grey-bearded face peering through the kitchen window.

The tradition is preserved in the annual children's anthology 'Bland tomtar och troll' (Among Gnomes and Trolls), first published in 1907 and still going today, which features stories collected from across the Swedish language area including Åland. The tomte represents the moral code of the traditional Åland farming community, where hard work and respect for the unseen were paramount — and where the line between the natural and the supernatural was as thin as the morning mist.

title: Tawa Creates the Worlds
summary: In the Hopi creation story, in the beginning only Tawa, the Sun Spirit, existed in endless space (Tokpella). Tawa formed the First World but its insect-like creatures lived unhappily in caves. To improve things, Tawa created Sotuknang, his nephew, who in turn created Spider Woman (Spider Grandmother) as a messenger and helper. Spider Woman was sent to lead the first creatures — then resembling insects — to the Second World, where they took on animal forms of wolves and bears. Still dissatisfied, Tawa created a Third World and Spider Woman guided the creatures there, where they finally became human. Spider Woman taught them weaving and pottery, and Hummingbird brought them the fire drill. This cycle of creation, destruction, and renewal through four worlds is central to Hopi cosmology, with humanity now living in the Fourth World.
source: Wikipedia: Hopi mythology; Barry Pritzker, The Hopi (2011); Harold Courlander, The Fourth World of the Hopis
full_text:
In the beginning, before the world had shape or name, only Tawa existed — the Sun Spirit, a being of pure light suspended in Tokpella, the Endless Space. There was no earth, no sky, no water. Only Tawa, burning quietly in the void like a coal that refuses to die.

Tawa formed the First World from his own light, shaping it the way a dreamer shapes a dream. The creatures that lived there were small and insect-like, burrowing in caves beneath a sky that had no sun. They were unhappy in their darkness, whispering to each other about the light they had never seen.

To help them, Tawa created his nephew Sotuknang — a being of structure and purpose. Sotuknang in turn created Spider Woman, Spider Grandmother, as a messenger and helper. She was ancient and wise, with legs like the rays of the dawn and eyes that could see in every direction at once.

Spider Woman gathered the First World creatures and led them to the Second World, where they took on the forms of wolves and bears. Still the world was not right — too wild, too cold, too full of teeth.

They climbed to the Third World, where the creatures finally became human. Spider Woman taught them to weave cloth and shape pottery. Hummingbird — a tiny, reckless being with iridescent wings — stole the fire drill from the fire spirits and brought it to the people. For the first time, they had warmth and cooked food.

But the people grew wicked. They fought. They forgot the prayers. And so the Third World was destroyed — in some versions by flood, in others by fire — and the survivors climbed through a hollow reed into the Fourth World, the world we know.

There they met Masauwu, the Spirit of Death and Earth God, who wore a mask that was both hideous and beautiful. He gave them the land and four sacred tablets — instructions for how to live, where to settle, and what ceremonies to perform. And the Fourth World began.

title: The Toad and the Snow Kachinas
summary: In Oraibi, the Snow Kachinas were practicing for a dance in the Chórzhovi kiva. North of the village at Katcínavala lived Toad Woman with her son. The boy often went to listen to the Kachinas sing. On the dance day, the Toad Boy painted his face and wore a wildcat robe. Children laughed at him and took him to an anthill because he liked ants. He ate the ants and returned to the plaza to enjoy the dance. When the children gave him red piki (paper bread) from the Kachinas, he brought it home to his mother. She was happy, and they ate it together. This story teaches about the inclusion of even the lowliest creatures in Kachina celebrations and demonstrates the Hopi value of kindness to those who are different.
source: H.R. Voth, The Traditions of the Hopi (1905); told by Kwáyeshva of Oraíbi
full_text:
In Oraibi, on Third Mesa, the Snow Kachinas were practicing for a dance in the Chórzhovi kiva. Their masks were white as the first frost, and their songs were the songs of winter — slow, deep, resonant with the weight of snow.

North of the village, at a place called Katcínavala, lived Toad Woman with her son. The boy was small and strange — his skin bumpy, his eyes too large, his manner quiet. He liked ants. He would sit for hours watching them carry seeds across the sand, marveling at their industry.

Every day, the boy crept to the kiva and pressed his ear against the stone wall, listening to the Kachinas sing. The music moved him in ways he could not explain. His feet tapped. His hands waved. He wanted to dance.

On the day of the dance, the Toad Boy painted his face with red ochre and wore a wildcat robe over his small, bumpy body. He walked to the plaza and stood among the children.

The children laughed at him. "Look at the Toad Boy!" they cried. "He thinks he can dance!" They grabbed him and carried him to an anthill, dumping him on top of it because he liked ants.

The boy sat on the anthill and ate the ants, one by one, while the dance continued. When the Kachinas finished, they gave the children red piki — thin, paper-like bread made from blue corn. The Toad Boy received a piece. He carried it home to his mother.

She was happy. They ate it together in their small lodge, the sweet, thin bread dissolving on their tongues.

This story teaches a Hopi value that runs deeper than it appears: inclusion. Even the lowliest creature — a toad boy who eats ants — has a place in the Kachina celebrations. The dance is not for the beautiful or the strong. It is for everyone. And the gift of piki, that thin red bread, is the gift of community itself.

title: Two Friends: Coyote and Bull Snake Exchange Visits
summary: Coyote and Bull Snake were friends who decided to visit each other's homes. Coyote visited Bull Snake first and found his burrow beautiful and comfortable. Bull Snake then visited Coyote's den. During the visit, Coyote played a trick on Bull Snake, or vice versa, depending on the version. The story humorously explores the nature of friendship across differences, the expectations of hospitality, and the consequences of deception between friends. It also incorporates elements of Hopi social values, including proper guest behavior and the responsibilities of hosts. The story ends with the two friends parting ways, each having learned something about trust and respect for different ways of living.
source: Harold Courlander, People of the Short Blue Corn (1993)
full_text:
Coyote and Bull Snake were friends — an unlikely pair, for Coyote was loud and restless while Bull Snake was quiet and still. But friendship, like rain, falls where it will.

Coyote visited Bull Snake first. He found the burrow beautiful — cool and dark, with walls that glowed faintly with embedded crystals. Bull Snake offered Coyote the best sleeping spot, the one near the back where the air was warmest.

"Now you must visit my den," Coyote said.

Bull Snake agreed and traveled to Coyote's home — a hollow under a rock, messy with old bones and scattered fur. Bull Snake was polite, though the smell was terrible.

During the visit, Coyote decided to play a trick. He told Bull Snake that the greatest honor in his den was to sleep in the deepest corner, where the air was thinnest. Bull Snake, trusting his friend, slithered into the deepest part of the den — and found himself stuck, his thick body wedged between two rocks.

Coyote laughed. "I've caught a snake!" he cried.

But Bull Snake did not laugh. He spoke quietly: "A friend who tricks his guest is no friend at all."

Coyote's laughter died. He helped Bull Snake out of the crevice, cleaning the dirt from his scales with his own paws. "I am sorry," he said, and for once, he meant it.

Bull Snake returned to his own burrow, and Coyote did not visit for a long time. When he finally did, he brought a gift — a fine piece of turquoise, smoothed by the river. Bull Snake accepted it, and the friendship resumed, though it was changed.

The story teaches Hopi values about hospitality and the responsibilities of hosts. A guest must be treated with respect, and a host who betrays that trust loses something that cannot be easily regained.

title: Tsichtinako Teaches the Sisters
summary: In the Acoma Pueblo creation story, Tsichtinako (Thought Woman) appeared as a voice guiding the sisters Iatiku and Nautsiti from within the earth. She couldn't be seen because she was a spirit without a human body. Tsichtinako instructed the sisters in all aspects of life: how to plant seeds from their baskets, how to make prayer sticks (pahos), how to conduct ceremonies, and how to organize their society into clans. She explained that Uchtsiti (the Sun, their father) had created the world but it was not yet complete, and the sisters were to complete it. Tsichtinako also taught them language, naming each plant, animal, and feature of the landscape. She established the four sacred directions and the relationship between the people and all beings. Tsichtinako continues to guide the Acoma people invisibly, representing the power of thought and the spiritual foundation of existence.
source: Edward Proctor Hunt, The Origin Myth of Acoma Pueblo (1928)
full_text:
Tsichtinako spoke from within the earth, a voice without a body, a mind without a face. The sisters Iatiku and Nautsiti could not see her, but they heard her as clearly as they heard the wind.

"Take the seeds from your baskets," Tsichtinako said, "and plant them in the earth. Each seed has a purpose. Corn will feed your children. Beans will climb the cornstalks and fix the soil. Squash will spread its leaves to shade the ground and keep the water from evaporating."

The sisters planted. They made prayer sticks — pahos — from reeds and feathers, and placed them at the four corners of their fields. Tsichtinako taught them how to arrange the prayers, how to face each direction, how to speak to the Sun Father and the Earth Mother.

"Name everything," Tsichtinako said. "The naming gives it power. Name the corn and it will grow. Name the rain and it will come. Name the directions — East, South, West, North — and the world will have order."

Iatiku named the plants. Nautsiti named the animals. Together they named the mountains and rivers, the clouds and winds, the stars and the shadows. Each name was a prayer, each prayer a thread connecting the people to the world.

Tsichtinako also taught them to organize their society into clans. The Corn Clan would tend the fields. The Kachina Clan would perform the ceremonies. The Arrow Clan would protect the village. Each clan had its duties, its responsibilities, its place in the web of relationships that held the community together.

Tsichtinako continues to guide the Acoma people invisibly. She is the power of thought itself — the ability to imagine a world that does not yet exist and bring it into being. She is the voice that speaks in the quiet moments, when a farmer looks at the sky and knows it will rain, or a mother holds her child and knows it will grow.

The Acoma people say: "Tsichtinako is always with us. We cannot see her, but we hear her in every thought that brings us closer to the truth."

title: The Trial of Lovers: Maiden of Matsaki
summary: A Zuni folk tale about the beautiful Maiden of Matsaki, desired by many suitors. After the war god Áhaiyúta and his brother courted her, they discovered she was cruel — she had let the children of Field-mice die of cold while she gambled. The gods punished her but also showed compassion for the helpless mouse children, taking them to their grandmother who raised them. The story teaches that even gods can be cruel, but those who find helpless children must care for them. The Maiden of Matsaki's story illustrates Zuni values about compassion, the consequences of cruelty, and the duty to care for orphans and vulnerable children. It also demonstrates that even divine beings are subject to moral judgment and that mercy can follow justice.
full_text:
The Maiden of Matsaki was beautiful — so beautiful that the war god Áhaiyúta and his brother Mátsailéma traveled from Thunder Mountain to court her. They arrived expecting to find a woman worthy of divine attention.

But the Maiden of Matsaki was cruel. The brothers discovered that she had let the children of Field-mice die of cold while she gambled with turquoise and shell beads. The mouse babies — tiny, naked, helpless — had cried through the night, and the Maiden had turned up the heat of her fire and laughed.

The war gods were enraged. Áhaiyúta struck the Maiden with his lightning bolt, and Mátsailéma sealed her fate with his thunder stone. The earth opened and swallowed her, and she was never seen again.

But the war gods did not stop there. They went to the place where the mouse children had died and found them still warm, their tiny hearts still beating. Despite their terrible nature — the war gods were known for their cruelty as much as their courage — they gathered the mouse babies and carried them to their grandmother on Thunder Mountain.

The grandmother took the orphaned mice and raised them. She fed them cornmeal and warm milk, she wove tiny blankets for their bodies, she sang them songs that only grandmothers know. The mice grew strong and healthy, and they never forgot the kindness of the war gods' grandmother.

"Even gods can be cruel," the story teaches. "But those who find helpless children must care for them. This is the law that binds the powerful to the weak, the divine to the mortal, the sky to the earth."

The Maiden of Matsaki's story is told to Zuni children as a warning against cruelty and gambling, and as a reassurance that the gods themselves — for all their power — are subject to moral judgment. Mercy can follow justice, and the cruelest beings can perform acts of tenderness.

title: Átahsaia the Cannibal Demon
summary: A Zuni legend about Átahsaia, a giant cannibal demon who terrorized the people. Átahsaia is described as a huge, monstrous being with burning eyes and an insatiable hunger for human flesh, especially children. The demon would descend from the mountains to raid villages, carrying off victims in a large basket on its back. The twin war gods Áhaiyúta and Mátsailéma confronted Átahsaia to save their people. They used their divine weapons and cunning to defeat the demon. In some versions, they tricked Átahsaia into falling into a pit of fire or into a canyon. The battle between the divine twins and the cannibal demon represents the eternal struggle between good and evil, order and chaos. After Átahsaia's defeat, the people were safe, but the story reminds Zuni children to be cautious and to respect the boundary between the civilized pueblo and the wild lands where dangerous spirits dwell.
source: Frank Cushing, Zuñi Folk Tales (1901); Wikipedia: Zuni mythology
full_text:
Átahsaia was a giant — so tall his head scraped the clouds, so wide his shadow covered entire villages. His eyes burned like coals, and his breath smelled of blood and old death. He lived in the mountains above Zuni country, and when hunger drove him down from his cave, the people hid.

He carried a basket on his back — a great woven thing as large as a house, lined with the bones of those he had already taken. Children were his favorite. He could smell them from miles away, could hear their heartbeats through the stone walls of their homes.

The people prayed to the twin war gods Áhaiyúta and Mátsailéma. "Save us," they cried. "Átahsaia grows bolder. He comes closer each night. Soon there will be no one left."

The twins climbed Thunder Mountain and looked down at the monster. They saw the trail of destruction — flattened houses, trampled fields, the scattered belongings of those Átahsaia had carried away.

Áhaiyúta spoke first. "We cannot fight him with weapons. He is too large. We must use cunning."

Mátsailéma agreed. They devised a plan. They built a great pit in the path Átahsaia always traveled, covering it with branches and earth so it looked like solid ground. At the bottom of the pit, they placed burning coals.

Then they sent a child — a brave girl with quick legs — to the edge of Átahsaia's cave. She danced and shouted until the monster rose from his sleep and charged. Átahsaia ran with terrifying speed, the ground shaking with each step.

The girl led him toward the pit. At the last moment, she leaped aside. Átahsaia, unable to stop, plunged into the pit. The coals erupted around him. He burned and thrashed, his roar shaking the mountains.

The twins stood at the edge and struck him with their lightning weapons until he lay still. His body fell into the canyon, and where he lay, the earth became scorched and red — a reminder of the monster who once terrorized the people.

After Átahsaia's defeat, the people were safe. But they remembered the lesson: the boundary between the civilized pueblo and the wild lands is not merely physical but spiritual. The wilderness holds dangerous spirits, and respect for that danger is the first protection against it.

title: The Two Little Ones and Their Turkeys
summary: A Zuni story about two orphaned children who were cared for by a flock of wild turkeys. The turkeys provided them with feathers for warmth, eggs for food, and protection from danger. The children lived in harmony with the turkeys, learning the ways of the forest and the language of birds. When the children grew older, they faced pressure to return to human society, but the turkeys warned them about the dangers of human greed. Eventually, the children had to choose between the freedom of the wild and the community of humans. The story explores themes of adoption — being raised by non-human caretakers — and the tension between wild and civilized life. The turkeys, like the deer in other Zuni stories, represent the generosity of the natural world and the reciprocal obligations between humans and animals.
full_text:
Two orphaned children wandered the wilderness, hungry and alone. Their parents had died in a fever that swept through the pueblo, and the relatives who should have cared for them were too consumed by their own grief to notice two small figures slipping away into the desert.

The children found shelter in a grove of piñon trees where a flock of wild turkeys lived. The turkeys watched the children with their round, bright eyes and felt something that turkeys do not often feel — pity.

The lead turkey, an old hen with feathers like bronze, approached the children. She offered them her warmth through the cold nights. She led them to nests where they could find eggs. She showed them which berries were safe and which were poison.

The children lived with the turkeys for many seasons. They learned the ways of the forest — the language of birds, the warnings of the wind, the signs that predicted rain. They grew strong on turkey eggs and piñon nuts, and they were happy.

But the turkeys warned them about the dangers of human greed. "People take without asking," the old hen said. "They hunt for sport, not for need. They wear feathers as decoration, not as honor."

The children knew this was true. They had seen it in the pueblo before their parents died.

When the children grew older, they faced pressure to return to human society. Hunters from the pueblo found them and tried to bring them back. The children were torn — the human world of their birth calling them one way, the turkey world of their raising calling them another.

They chose to return to the pueblo, but they carried the turkeys' teachings with them. They taught the people to honor the turkeys, to ask permission before hunting, to waste nothing of what the bird gives.

The turkeys, for their part, continued to live in the grove, generous and watchful. They represent the generosity of the natural world and the reciprocal obligations between humans and animals — obligations that exist whether we acknowledge them or not.

title: The Thunderbird Wakinyan
summary: Wakinyan is the great Thunderbird of Lakota mythology, a powerful sky spirit associated with thunder, lightning, and storms. His flapping wings create thunderclaps and his eyes flash lightning. When Unhcegila emerged from the primordial waters to flood the land, Wakinyan flapped his wings to dry the earth and shot lightning to destroy the serpent's heart. The Thunderbird represents the destructive yet renewing power of storms and is considered one of the most potent spirits. Wakinyan is also associated with the west direction and is a protector of the Lakota people against chaos and disorder.
full_text:
Wakinyan — the Thunderbird — is the great sky spirit of Lakota mythology, a being of such power that even the other spirits treat him with caution. His body is massive, spanning the width of the sky when his wings are spread. His feathers are red and gold, and his eyes flash with the lightning that is his weapon and his voice.

When Wakinyan flaps his wings, thunderclaps shake the earth. When he opens his eyes, lightning bolts split the sky. When he speaks, his voice is the rumble that precedes the storm.

Wakinyan is the protector of the Lakota people against chaos and disorder. He is the eternal enemy of the great water serpents — Unhcegila and her kind — who lurk in the depths of lakes and rivers, waiting to devour the unwary.

When Unhcegila emerged from the primordial waters to flood the land, it was Wakinyan who rose to meet her. He flapped his wings to dry the earth, his feathers sending waves of heat across the plains. He shot lightning at the serpent's heart, the red crystal that was her weakness.

The battle was terrible. The sky turned black with Wakinyan's wings. The earth shook with Unhcegila's thrashing. Lightning and water clashed in a storm that lasted four days and four nights.

Finally, Wakinyan's lightning struck the crystal. The serpent's heart shattered, and she fell. Her body became the Badlands — the eroded, twisted landscape that the Lakota call Makhóšiča, the Bad Lands, where her bones still jut from the earth like fingers reaching for the sky.

Wakinyan is associated with the west direction, where storms come from. He is honored with tobacco offerings, and his rumbling voice is heard whenever he pursues evil spirits across the sky. The Lakota say that when thunder rolls, Wakinyan is speaking — warning the monsters below that the Thunderbird is watching, that the protector of the people is on patrol.

title: Tobacco Society: Chief No Vitals Discovers Tobacco
summary: The Crow people believe that tobacco was first discovered by Chief No Vitals at Devils Lake in eastern North Dakota. The Creator instructed him to seek the sacred plant, telling him that the worship of tobacco would help the Crow honor God and maintain their connection to the spirit world. Chief No Vitals found the plant and brought it back to his people, establishing the Tobacco Society (Bacu'sua). The society ensures that all rites and rituals for cultivating tobacco are performed correctly. Smoking tobacco is believed to carry prayers directly to God, as the smoke ascends to the heavens. The sacred pipe society uses tobacco daily to maintain closeness with the Creator.
full_text:
A Crow woman dreamed that a great flood was coming. She told the elders, but they did not believe her. She prepared anyway — gathering food, building a raft, teaching her children to swim.

When the flood came, it was devastating. The rivers rose and covered the plains. The lodges were swept away. The people scrambled for higher ground.

The woman and her family survived on the raft she had built. She guided them to a hilltop where other survivors gathered. When the waters receded, they returned to the plains and rebuilt.

The woman was honored as a prophet, and the elders learned to listen to the dreams of women, for dreams are messages from the spirits.

title: Tirawa Creates the Universe
summary: Tirawa (Atíʼas Tirawa), 'Our Father Above,' was the supreme creator god of the Pawnee. He created the universe and placed the Morning Star in the East and the Evening Star in the West. The Morning Star, a male warrior god, was created first. The female Evening Star resisted the divine plan to create humankind, so Morning Star fought and overcame forces in the western sky with his fireball to mate with her. The first human thus created was a girl. Tirawa taught the Pawnee tattooing, fire-building, hunting, agriculture, speech, clothing, religious rituals, and sacrifice. His wife was Atira (Mother Corn), goddess of the Earth.
full_text:
Tirawa Atíʼas Tirawa, 'Our Father Above,' was the supreme creator god of the Pawnee. He created the universe and placed the Morning Star in the East and the Evening Star in the West. The Morning Star, red and fierce, represented masculine power and war. The Evening Star, pale and gentle, represented feminine wisdom and fertility. Together they governed all creation.

Tirawa was invisible — a presence felt in the wind, heard in the thunder, seen in the lightning that split the sky. He did not walk among the people, for no mortal eye could bear his radiance. But he spoke through the stars, through the movements of the planets, through the cycles of the seasons.

The Pawnee believed that Tirawa placed the stars in the sky as a living map, a guide for every aspect of life. When to plant corn, when to hunt buffalo, when to make war, when to make peace — all was written in the stars. The priests were trained to read these signs, their eyes tracing the patterns of light that Tirawa had set in motion since the beginning of time.

Tirawa was both creator and sustainer. He was the force that kept the earth turning, the sun rising, the rain falling. He was the breath in every living thing, the warmth in every fire, the strength in every warrior's arm. The Pawnee did not worship Tirawa with temples or altars. They worshipped him by living in harmony with the stars he had placed in the sky.

title: The Three Sisters: Corn, Beans, and Squash
summary: In Iroquois tradition, the Three Sisters are the agricultural spirits Corn (Onatah), Beans, and Squash. They are inseparable companions who grow best when planted together. According to legend, the Creator gave these three plants to the people as a sacred gift. Corn provides a stalk for the beans to climb, beans fix nitrogen in the soil for the corn, and squash spreads its broad leaves to shade the ground, preventing weeds and retaining moisture. The sisters represent the principle of mutual support and cooperation that underlies Haudenosaunee society. Ceremonies honor them throughout the growing season, especially the Green Corn Festival when the first corn ripens.
full_text:
The Three Sisters are the agricultural spirits Corn — Onatah — Beans, and Squash. They are inseparable companions who grow best when planted together, each one supporting the others in a dance of mutual aid that mirrors the principles of Haudenosaunee society.

Corn is the eldest. She grows tall and strong, her stalk rising like a pillar toward the sky. Beans climbs the cornstalk, using it as a trellis. In return, beans fix nitrogen in the soil, enriching the earth for corn's roots.

Squash spreads her broad leaves across the ground, shading the soil and preventing weeds from growing. Her sharp spines protect the other sisters from animals that would eat their fruit.

Together, the Three Sisters produce a complete diet — corn for carbohydrates, beans for protein, squash for vitamins. They are the foundation of Haudenosaunee agriculture, and their planting is accompanied by ceremonies that honor their spirits.

The Green Corn Festival celebrates the first ripening of the corn. The people dance, sing, and feast. They offer the first ears of corn to the spirits, thanking the Three Sisters for their gift.

The Three Sisters represent the principle of mutual support and cooperation that underlies Haudenosaunee society. Just as the plants support each other, so must the people support each other — each clan, each family, each individual contributing to the strength of the whole.

The story teaches that independence is not the absence of interdependence, and that the strongest communities are those in which each member supports and is supported by the others.

title: The Thunderers (Hadiwennoda:dye's)
summary: The Thunderers are powerful storm spirits who live in the sky and cause thunder and lightning. They are described as giant warriors who hunt and kill the great horned serpents and other monsters that threaten humanity. In the Seneca tradition, they are led by the great chief Hino. Their gaze can bring death to mortal men, yet they are generally benevolent and play a protective role in Iroquois legends. They are the eternal enemies of the Great Horned Serpent Oniare and maintain the balance of the world by ensuring no monster grows too powerful. The Thunderers are honored with tobacco offerings, and their rumbling voices are heard whenever they pursue evil spirits across the sky.
source: native-languages.org; Smith - Myths of the Iroquois
full_text:
The Thunderers are powerful storm spirits who live in the sky and cause thunder and lightning. They are described as giant warriors who hunt and kill the great horned serpents and other monsters that threaten humanity.

In the Seneca tradition, they are led by the great chief Hino, whose voice is the thunder that rolls across the sky and whose weapon is the lightning bolt that splits the darkest clouds. When Hino speaks, his voice shakes the mountains. When he strikes, his lightning illuminates the entire sky.

The Thunderers' gaze can bring death to mortal men, yet they are generally benevolent and play a protective role in Iroquois legends. They are the eternal enemies of the Great Horned Serpent Oniare, who lurks in the deepest waters and threatens to destroy the world.

The Thunderers are honored with tobacco offerings, and their rumbling voices are heard whenever they pursue evil spirits across the sky. When a thunderstorm rolls in, the people know that the Thunderers are at work, clearing the sky of monsters and restoring order to the world.

title: Turtle Island: The Lenape Earth Diver
summary: In the Lenape creation account, before land existed, all the animals lived in deep water. They grew weary of swimming and wanted dry land. One by one the animals dove to retrieve earth from the bottom — the otter, the beaver — but each failed, gasping for air. Finally the humble muskrat took his turn. He was under the water so long the others thought he had drowned. At last he surfaced, near death, with a tiny clump of mud in his paw. He Who Creates Us By Thought summoned Turtle to the surface and placed the mud on Turtle's back. The Creator caused the mud to grow and spread across Turtle's shell, forming Turtle Island, the North American continent. From a tree growing on this new land sprouted the first man and woman, the ancestors of all people.
source: Nanticoke Lenape Museum resources; Brinton - The Lenape and Their Legends; native-languages.org
full_text:
In the Lenape creation account, before land existed, all the animals lived in deep water. They swam through the darkness, their bodies adapting to the cold and the pressure. But they grew weary of swimming. They wanted dry land — a place to rest, to build, to live.

One by one, the animals dove to retrieve earth from the bottom of the ocean. The otter went first, his sleek body cutting through the water. He dove deep, his lungs burning, but he surfaced with nothing — the ocean floor was too far below.

The beaver went next, his powerful tail driving him downward. He dove deeper than the otter, past the light, past the warmth, into the cold blackness. He surfaced gasping, his paws empty.

Others tried — the turtle, the muskrat, the loon. Each failed. The ocean was too deep, the darkness too thick.

Finally, the humble muskrat took his turn. He was the smallest of all the animals, the weakest. The others mocked him. "If the beaver could not do it, how can you?"

The muskrat said nothing. He dove.

He was under the water so long the others thought he had drowned. They gathered at the surface, their eyes wet with tears, their bodies preparing to mourn.

At last he surfaced, near death, with a tiny clump of mud in his paw.

He Who Creates Us By Thought summoned Turtle to the surface and placed the mud on Turtle's back. The Creator caused the mud to grow and spread across Turtle's shell, forming Turtle Island, the North American continent.

From a tree growing on this new land sprouted the first man and woman, the ancestors of all people. And the muskrat, who had given everything for a tiny piece of earth, was honored as the hero of creation.

title: Tabaldak Creates Glooscap and Malsumis
summary: In Abenaki tradition, the Great Spirit Tabaldak first created the world and all the people. When he finished making humans, he wiped the dust from his hands, and from this divine dust were born twin brothers — Glooscap and Malsumis. Glooscap was given the power to create a good world, full of kind animals, sweet fruits, and gentle rivers. Malsumis, the wolf, was his opposite, creating only evil — dangerous animals, thorns, and crooked rivers that flooded the land. From birth, Malsumis resented his brother and plotted to destroy him. Glooscap discovered that his brother could only be killed by a blow from a fern root. Malsumis tricked the animals into revealing this secret and attacked Glooscap, but the good twin was saved by Grandmother Woodchuck. Glooscap eventually defeated Malsumis and turned him into stone, where he remains, the embodiment of all that is harmful in nature.
full_text:
In Abenaki tradition, the Great Spirit Tabaldak first created the world and all the people. When he finished making humans, he wiped the dust from his hands, and from this divine dust were born twin brothers — Glooscap (also called Gluskabe) and Malsumis.

Glooscap was good and creative. He shaped the mountains and rivers, the forests and meadows. He made the animals and taught them to live in harmony with the people. He created the seasons — spring, summer, autumn, winter — so that the world would be ever-changing, ever-renewing.

Malsumis was destructive and jealous. He made the wolves and the serpents, the thorns and the poison ivy. He created the storms and the earthquakes, the droughts and the floods. He was angry that his brother's creations were loved and his were feared.

The brothers fought. Glooscap defeated Malsumis and banished him to the underworld. But Malsumis's creations remained — the wolves still howl, the serpents still strike, the storms still rage. They are the necessary counterbalance to Glooscap's goodness.

Tabaldak watched the conflict between his sons and was satisfied. The world needed both — the creative force of Glooscap and the destructive force of Malsumis. Without destruction, there could be no renewal. Without darkness, light would have no meaning.

The Abenaki tell this story to explain the dual nature of existence — the presence of both good and evil, creation and destruction, in every aspect of life.

title: The Thunder Beings (Aniyvdaqualosgi) (Cherokee)
summary: The Cherokee believe in the Thunder Beings, known as Aniyvdaqualosgi or Ani-Yuntikwalaski. The Great Thunder and his two sons, the Thunder Boys, live in the land of the west above the sky vault. They dress in lightning and rainbows. Unlike many tribes where thunder spirits take bird form, Cherokee Thunderers are human in form — powerful and dangerous but generally friendly to humans. The priests pray to the Thunder beings for rain and blessings. Some lesser thunder beings live closer to the Earth's surface in cliffs, mountains, and waterfalls, and these are more mischievous, sometimes causing harm. Thunder is said to be the sound of the Great Thunder's wings or his voice rolling across the sky. Lightning is the fire from his eyes.
source: Wikipedia - Cherokee spiritual beliefs; Mooney, Myths of the Cherokee
full_text:
When the sky darkens and the thunder rolls across the mountains like the drums of war, the Cherokee do not cower. They listen. They stand at their doorways and look to the west, where the storm comes from, and they say, "The Aniyvdaqualosgi are riding."

The Thunder Beings — Aniyvdaqualosgi, or Ani-Yuntikwalaski — are among the most powerful spirits in the Cherokee world. They are not abstractions, not metaphors, not the random collisions of atmospheric forces. They are beings — alive, conscious, and purposeful — who ride the storm clouds in forms so magnificent that the human eye can barely hold them.

The greatest of the Thunder Beings is the Great Thunder, known as Galun'lati. He is human in form, unlike the bird-shaped thunder spirits of many other tribes. He stands at the center of the storm, dressed in lightning and rainbows, his body crackling with energy, his eyes flashing with the fire that men call lightning. Beside him ride his two sons — the Thunder Boys — younger and fiercer, their voices splitting the sky like axes splitting wood.

The Thunder Beings live in the west, above the sky vault, in a land where the clouds are solid ground and the rain falls upward. Their house is built of living lightning, its walls pulsing with color, its roof a dome of perpetual thunder. There, in the land above the world, they prepare for their journeys across the earth.

When the Thunder Beings ride, the sky transforms. Clouds gather like armies, dark and massive, their bellies purple with stored lightning. The wind rises, carrying the smell of rain and the electric charge that makes the hair stand on end. Then the first thunder cracks — not a rumble but a report, sharp and absolute, as if the sky itself had been split open with a blade.

Lightning is the fire from the Great Thunder's eyes. It strikes the earth with purpose — not randomly, not randomly, but with the precision of a hunter's arrow. It strikes the places that need cleansing, the trees that harbor evil spirits, the rocks where malevolent forces have gathered. When the lightning strikes, it leaves behind the smell of ozone and the faint outline of the Thunder Being's handprint, burned into the stone.

The priests of the Cherokee pray to the Thunder Beings for rain and blessings. They build altars on the high ridges, where the storms pass closest to the earth, and they lay offerings of tobacco and white bead. They sing the songs that the Thunder Beings taught the first medicine men — songs of power, songs of petition, songs that ride the wind like birds.

But not all Thunder Beings are friendly. The lesser Thunderers — those who live closer to the earth, in the cliffs and waterfalls and mountain clefts — are more dangerous. They are mischievous, sometimes cruel. They hurl rocks from the cliffs. They stir up flash floods. They send lightning to strike the unwary. The priests warn that these lesser spirits must be propitiated with offerings and respect, for they are jealous and easily angered.

There is a story of a man who climbed to the top of a waterfall during a storm, seeking to steal a feather from the Great Thunder's headdress. The Thunder Boys saw him and were amused at first, for no mortal had ever been so bold. But when the man reached for the feather, the Great Thunder turned his gaze upon him, and the man felt the full weight of the storm — the wind, the rain, the lightning, the thunder — pressing down on him like the palm of a giant hand.

The man fell from the waterfall and was killed. His body was found at the base of the falls, unmarked by lightning but twisted in a way that suggested he had been squeezed by something impossibly large. The priests said that the Great Thunder had granted him a swift death, which was more mercy than he deserved.

The Thunder Beings are neither good nor evil. They are power — raw, elemental, and ancient. They bring the rain that makes the corn grow and the lightning that purifies the air. They are the warriors of the sky, the defenders of the cosmic order, and the friends of those who approach them with humility and respect. When the storm comes, the Cherokee stand at their doorways and watch, and they remember that the world is bigger than they are, and more powerful, and that the beings who ride the clouds are watching over them.

title: Tlanuwa: The Giant Raptor (Cherokee)
summary: Tlanuwa is a giant mythological bird of prey with feathers made of impenetrable metal. This massive raptor could carry off humans and even small deer in its talons. Its feathers were said to be sharp as knives and could be launched as projectiles. The Tlanuwa lived in the highest mountain peaks and remote cliffs. In Cherokee legend, the Tlanuwa sometimes battled the Uktena serpent, their ancient enemy. The birds were also known to fight against humans who invaded their territory. The Tlanuwa appears in stories from many Southeastern tribes including the Creek and Natchez, suggesting it was a widespread figure in the regional mythology. Some accounts describe it as a benevolent protector spirit of the Cherokee people.
source: Wikipedia - Cherokee spiritual beliefs; native-languages.org Tlanuwa
full_text:
